query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During concurrent wear and corrosion of a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy at elevated temperature, repetitive disruption and re-formation of phase-specific oxide films—particularly at phase boundaries with galvanic potential differentials—causes a cyclic synergy. Mechanical sliding ruptures the protective oxide layers, exposing fresh high-energy sites. Localized galvanic couples then accelerate selective dissolution in newly exposed regions, leading to rapid oxide re-formation. Repeated mechanical removal of these semi-protective oxides ultimately amplifies total material loss beyond the sum of individual wear and corrosion acting separately.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase (e.g., B2 + L12 or FCC + σ) eutectic high-entropy alloy with nominal passivating oxide films formed under elevated-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to simultaneous mechanical sliding in a corrosive environment at elevated temperature, so that tribological contact disrupts oxide films and promotes localized dissolution near phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature above the oxide-formation threshold, in a chemically aggressive environment (e.g., chloride-containing environment), under typical tribological loads where moderate to severe wear occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase-specific galvanic microcouples (e.g., FCC vs. σ) and their oxide films, which form and break down repeatedly under sliding contact.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical abrasion disrupts protective oxides and locally depassivates the alloy, allowing faster electrochemical attack near phase boundaries. This accelerates selective dissolution, leading to a repeated cycle of oxide breakdown and reformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The total degradation rate (mass loss or wear volume) will exceed the sum of wear-only plus corrosion-only rates by an estimated factor of at least 2–3 under these conditions. Both wear damage and corrosion-related metal loss individually increase relative to their single-process baselines, as the synergy magnifies localized dissolution and mechanical removal of newly exposed material.
generation.baseline: Separate wear testing of the alloy in an inert environment (no corrosion), and separate immersion corrosion testing with minimal mechanical stress. Under these baseline conditions, material loss should be lower than under the combined tribo-corrosion scenario.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism applies when the alloy can form at least partially protective oxides at elevated temperatures yet remains vulnerable to phase-specific galvanic coupling and mechanical disruption (e.g., moderate–high temperature oxidation, in corrosive media with sliding contact). Under conditions with negligible oxide formation or minimal galvanic potential differences, this synergy should be much less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The specific contribution of each distinct phase to the overall galvanic coupling and wear–corrosion synergy is not fully quantified, and may vary with minor changes in alloy chemistry, temperature, and loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two sets of elevated-temperature pin-on-disk tribo-corrosion tests in a chloride-containing environment, one set using a multi-phase HEA and another using a similar composition homogenized (single-phase) alloy with reduced galvanic coupling potential. Collect real-time electrochemical and friction data during sliding and measure total mass loss afterward.
measurements: Electrochemical current density during sliding (to probe corrosion rates).
Friction coefficient and wear track morphology from in situ imaging methods.
Post-test mass or volume loss (gravimetric or profilometric).
Surface chemistry and oxide film characteristics via SEM/EDS or XPS.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase alloy under simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions does not exhibit a significantly higher total degradation rate than the single-phase reference (and than the independent sum of wear-only and corrosion-only contributions), the proposed synergy mechanism is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.

decision.trend: Early work (2014) introduced AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEAs with promising strength/ductility, establishing multi-phase lamellar microstructures. Subsequent (2022) corrosion-focused studies on this same composition documented temperature-dependent passivity but did not resolve how mechanical wear might disrupt oxide films. More recent (2025) efforts evaluated combined wear and corrosion performance in AlCoCrFeNi-based alloys, aiming to mitigate synergistic degradation but without fully clarifying the fundamental mechanistic coupling of wear and corrosion at high temperatures in multi-phase EHEAs.
decision.unsolved: Despite microstructural refinements and passivation studies, how mechanical wear and corrosive processes mutually accelerate material removal in elevated-temperature service remains unclear. The interplay of oxide film disruption, multi-phase galvanic interactions, and repeated mechanical damage to freshly exposed surfaces is not yet fully understood, and no single unifying mechanism has been firmly established for these alloys.
decision.lever: Perform real-time tribo-corrosion testing at elevated temperature using in-situ imaging (e.g., high-temperature SEM) and electrochemical methods to monitor oxide film formation, breakdown, and local dissolution on different phases as wear proceeds, while varying normal load and test atmosphere.
decision.why: Direct observation of how wear disrupts protective oxides and how corrosion alters surface films is needed to pinpoint a single dominant synergy mechanism for multi-phase eutectic HEAs. Monitoring oxide breakdown and reformation under dynamic contact in a reactive environment can distinguish whether film disruption and re-oxidation cycles drive the accelerated degradation.
